What the model says

Across 232 qualified MLB hitters in 2026, at equal swing length, contact and whiff rate, +1 mph of bat speed is associated with +10 points of xwOBA, and +1 point of squared-up rate with +4 points. The swing metrics explain 42% of the differences in production between hitters; adding swing decisions (chase and in-zone swing rates) raises it to 47%. The rest comes from timing, launch direction and factors public data does not capture.

These are cross-sectional associations, not guarantees: they set the hypothesis to test with the player, not the expected outcome.

Development plan

Diagnosis. Alejandro Kirk’s contact is elite (91st percentile in squared-up rate, 92nd in whiff avoidance), but his bat speed (71.6 mph, 43rd percentile) caps the damage on contact: 88 mph average exit velocity, 3.7% barrels.

Priority. Add bat speed while protecting contact quality.

  1. Screen – Is bat speed limited by physical capacity or by sequencing? Force-plate profile (CMJ, IMTP: peak force, RFD, asymmetries) and rotational med-ball throw, read alongside the biomechanics data (kinematic sequence, lead-leg block, hip-shoulder separation).
  2. Intervene – If capacity-limited: lower-body force and rotational power block. If sequencing-limited: intent-based swings, overload/underload bat training with the hitting coaches.
  3. Monitor – Bat speed and squared-up rate each week (cage, BP, games). Red flag: squared-up rate dropping by more than 3 points as speed rises.

Data: Baseball Savant, public Statcast data (bat tracking, expected stats, exit velocity). Bat speed = average of the top 90% of competitive swings. Percentiles (1–100), model and profiles are based on the 232 qualified MLB hitters in 2026 (570+ competitive swings). Profiles: k-means on bat speed, swing length, squared-up and whiff rates. Internal biomechanics data would replace the screening hypotheses with measured values. Report: Hugo Leligny.
